props.title: The Day After Trinity
props.initialSlug: The birth of the atomic age.

sections.content: **The Day After Trinity (1981)** (1981) stands as one of the most haunting documentaries about the atomic age, focusing on J. Robert Oppenheimer and the Manhattan Project. Director Jon Else crafted a devastating portrait that combines rare archival footage with intimate interviews of the scientists who created the atomic bomb. The film's power comes from capturing Oppenheimer's transformation from ambitious physicist to tortured humanitarian, crystallized in his famous quote referencing the Bhagavad Gita: "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds."

sections.content: The ethical implications of scientific advancement emerged as a major documentary theme following **The Day After Trinity**. **Radio Bikini** (1988) exposed the devastating effects of nuclear testing on Pacific Islanders and American servicemen, while **Into Eternity** (2010) contemplates the 100,000-year future of nuclear waste storage. These films share Trinity's central question: what are the moral responsibilities of scientists whose work can both advance and destroy civilization?

The atomic age spawned a wave of science documentaries examining humanity's relationship with technology. **The World at War** (1973) dedicated episodes to the bombing of Japan, while **White Light/Black Rain** (2007) provided searing testimony from Hiroshima survivors. **Particle Fever** (2013) shows modern physics' pursuit of the Higgs boson, carrying echoes of the Manhattan Project's race for scientific breakthrough. SUBHEAD: The Human Cost of Scientific Progress

movies.title: Countdown to Zero
movies.slug: Traces the history and ongoing threat of nuclear weapons, featuring interviews with world leaders and experts

sections.content: Beyond nuclear weapons, films like **A Brief History of Time** (1991) and **The Theory of Everything** (2014) explore the personal toll of scientific genius. But **The Day After Trinity** remains uniquely powerful for showing how the brightest minds of a generation grappled with unleashing unprecedented destructive power. The film's interviews with Manhattan Project scientists like Hans Bethe and Robert Wilson reveal their initial excitement giving way to horror - a pattern that would repeat with later technological breakthroughs explored in **AlphaGo** (2017) and **The Social Dilemma** (2020).
